title: Rebel verbs
goal: Master the past participles of irregular verbs — a small group that happens to be the most used every day.
bekal: using the twenty-two most important irregular verbs
telling what happened yesterday without tripping over the forms
wave: Go back to **unit 16**: name ten things you like and dislike, each with the right form — *houden van*, *leuk vinden*, *lekker vinden*, *graag*.

dialogs.title: Dialog — Wat is er gebeurd?
dialogs.intro: Budi arrives late, soaking wet, and without his bike.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Wat is er gebeurd? Je bent doorweekt!
lines.literal: what is there happened? you are soaked!

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: No way! Where was it parked?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bij het station. Ik heb hem op slot gezet, echt waar.
lines.id: At the station. I locked it, honestly.
lines.literal: at the station. I have him on lock put, really true.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Dan weet je het nu. Heb je aangifte gedaan?
lines.id: Well, now you know. Did you report it?
lines.literal: then know you it now. have you report done?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, ik ben naar het bureau gegaan. Ze hebben gelachen.
lines.id: Yes, I went to the police station. They laughed.
lines.literal: yes, I am to the station gone. they have laughed.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Logisch. Er zijn vorig jaar bijna een miljoen fietsen gestolen.
lines.id: Makes sense. Last year almost a million bikes were stolen.
lines.literal: logical. there are last-year almost a million bikes stolen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Een miljoen? Dat heb ik niet geweten.
lines.id: A million? I didn't know that.
lines.literal: a million? that have I not known.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Koop een tweedehandsfiets. En twee sloten.
lines.id: Buy a second-hand bike. And two locks.
lines.literal: buy a second-hand-bike. and two locks.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik heb mijn les geleerd. Op de moeilijke manier.
lines.id: I've learned my lesson. The hard way.
lines.literal: I have my lesson learned. on the hard way.

notes: **Wat is er gebeurd?** — *gebeuren* takes *zijn*, not *hebben*. Which verbs take which is covered fully in the next unit.
**Gestolen** from *stelen* (to steal) — vowel pattern e → o, just like English *steal → stolen*. Sadly, it's one of the words newcomers to the Netherlands learn fastest.
**Waar stond hij?** — *stond* is the simple past of *staan*. This form (the *imperfectum*) is used for some verbs even in conversation; the list is in unit 19.
**Echt waar** = "really, truly". Used to insist, and also as an incredulous question: *Echt waar?*
**Aangifte doen** = to report to the police. For a stolen bike you can file online — and you should, because insurers ask for it.
**Ze hebben gelachen** — *lachen* ends in *ch*, but it's a **strong** verb: its participle is *gelachen*, not *gelacht*. The 't kofschip rule only applies to weak verbs.

**Bijna een miljoen fietsen** — a real figure; somewhere between 700,000 and a million bikes are stolen in the Netherlands each year. That's why expensive bikes are rarely ridden to work, and a *tweedehandsfiets* is the normal choice, not a last resort.
**Dat heb ik niet geweten** — from *weten*. This form is a bit formal; in conversation people more often say *dat wist ik niet*.

grammars.title: Recurring vowel patterns
body: Dutch irregular verbs aren't entirely random: most follow a handful of shared vowel changes, a heritage also visible in English and German.
after: As an English speaker, you'll find many of these familiar: *drink-drank-drunk* ↔ *drinken-dronk-gedronken*, *write-wrote-written* ↔ *schrijven-schreef-geschreven*. The kinship is real, and you can use it as a memory bridge.
The mark of a strong verb's participle: it ends in **-en**, not *-t/-d* — just like English *written*, *spoken*. That's the quickest way to spot one.
Don't try to memorize the whole list at once. Learn the **twenty or so** used most — listed on the next page — and the rest will stick on their own through use.

grammars.title: The essential twenty-two
body: These are the verbs that come up in almost every conversation. Their participles stand at the end of the sentence.
after: ⚠️ *Kopen → gekocht*, *brengen → gebracht*, *denken → gedacht*, *zoeken → gezocht*: a small group ending in *-cht* — compare English *bought*, *brought*, *thought*, *sought*. All four are very common, so learn them together.
*Begrijpen* and *verliezen* have a fixed prefix, so no *ge-*: *begrepen*, *verloren*.

blocks.text: The most effective way to learn strong verbs isn't rereading the list but using them in sentences about yourself. Take ten verbs from the list on the previous page and complete these sentences:

blocks.title: Past-tense sentences you'll need most
items: *Heb je goed geslapen?* — Did you sleep well?
*Ik heb het niet begrepen.* — I didn't understand.
*Wat heb je gezegd?* — What did you say?
*Ik heb mijn sleutels verloren.* — I've lost my keys.
*Hij heeft me geholpen.* — He helped me.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: I've reported it to the police.
Ik heb mijn telefoon laten vallen.

blocks.text: *Kwijt zijn* (to have lost) is far more common in daily life than *verliezen*: *Ik ben mijn sleutels kwijt.* When it turns up again: *Ik heb ze weer gevonden.*

The emergency number in the Netherlands is **112** for urgent situations and **0900-8844** for the police in non-emergencies — a stolen bike, for example. Operators almost always speak English, but opening with *Spreekt u Engels?* in Dutch still makes everything go more smoothly.
